newsitem.title: USA: General Mills must permit Chex competition - FTC.
newsitem.headline: General Mills must permit Chex competition - FTC.

text.p: The Federal Trade Commission announced Thursday it has prevented the price of Chex brand cold cereals from rising, by setting conditions on an acquisition by General Mills Inc.

General Mills acquired Chex brand cereal from Ralcorp Holdings. Ralcorp was permitted to retain its private label bands -- which produce substantially the same products under grocery or wholesaler names -- but with major restrictions. The FTC voted 3-2 to require as a condition of the acquisition that General Mills permit Ralcorp's private label brands to compete without restrictions.
The competition would be caried out by Ralcorp's "New Ralcorp" entity.

"Conditions attached to clearing the merger are designed to eliminate fully and immediately any barriers to New Ralcorp competing aggressively in promoting private label products," said FTC Chairman Robert Pitofsky in a statement.

Before the FTC required a change, the original agreement permitted New Ralcorp to manufacture and sell Chex cereals only 18 months after the deal. In addition, General Mills had to agree before anyone else could manufacture and sell private label cereals identical to Chex products.
The FTC said that neither of those restrictions could stand because they would have set barriers to others trying to compete, resulting in higher prices on Chex cereals.

General Mills, based in Minneapolis, Minn., is acquiring the name brand breakfast cereal and snack mix business of Ralcorp Holdings for $570 million. Ralcorp Holdings was created by Ralston Purina Co in 1994 to license Ralston Purina technology.
The FTC had said General Mills' acquisition of the branded cereal business of Ralcorp would boost its share of the U.S. breakfast cereal market to 31 percent.

Roscoe Starek, a Federal Trade Commissioner who dissented, said consumers have many alternatives if a brekfast cereal producer raises prices. He said it was "completely unnecessary" to have the FTC agreement.
Commissioner Mary Azcuenaga dissented in part, opposing elimination of the 18-month non-competitive clause in the merger.
